title: Palantir is one of just 3 crushed S&P 500 stocks up for the year
detail:
Palantir is one of just 3 crushed S&P 500 stocks up for the year
Opeyemi Babalola, Celine Provini
Tue, October 27, 2026 at 9:33 AM MST 6 min read
^GSPC
PLTR
NOW
PTC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Anyone who has held a stock through a crash knows the relief of seeing it climb again. It feels like the damage is undone. Usually it isn't. A stock that loses half its value must double just to break even.

That math is playing out across the S&P 500. The index's 25 worst performers fell an average of 42.4% in the first half, according to Bespoke Investment Group data cited by Seeking Alpha. Since July, they've rebounded 34.6%. Bespoke described the group as a mix of consumer stocks and software names that investors expected AI to make obsolete.

Yet the group is still down about 22% for the year. A big rally on a shrunken base does not refill the hole.

Measured from 2025 closing prices, only three of the 25 are up for the year. They are Palantir Technologies (PLTR), ServiceNow (NOW), and PTC (PTC), and each got there a different way.

Also read: Vanguard's S&P 500 fund outruns its own rising dividend

Palantir earned its comeback with a blowout quarter

Palantir, which sells data software to governments and businesses, began 2026 at 155 times trailing earnings, according to 24/7 Wall St. Shares slid even as first-quarter revenue grew 85% because investors doubted the price, not the business.

The second quarter changed that debate. Revenue jumped 93% to $1.94 billion, according to Palantir's earnings release. It also lifted its full-year forecast to about $8.15 billion, and CEO Alex Karp called the quarter "otherworldly."

Palantir is up about 12% for 2026. It trades about 6% below its 52-week high of $212.94 and far above its low of $106.37, according to StockAnalysis.

Valuation is the catch. Palantir trades at about 105 times expected earnings. Its 30 analysts rate it a Buy, with a $207.62 average target. That leaves little upside before results on Monday, Nov. 2, which already face a high bar.

Palantir, ServiceNow, and PTC are the only three of the S&P 500's 25 worst first-half performers now trading above their 2025 closing prices.asbe / Getty Images
ServiceNow's cushion is thin heading into earnings

ServiceNow, whose software runs IT and HR tasks at big companies, took two hits.

First came the "SaaSpocalypse," a sell-off on fears that businesses would build their own software with AI. S&P 500 software stocks fell more than 26% from late January to April, Reuters reported.

The second hit was its own. Shares fell nearly 15% on April 23, after ServiceNow blamed delayed Middle East deals for slower subscription growth, according to Reuters.

Results repaired the damage. Second quarter subscription revenue rose 24.5% to $3.88 billion, and the company raised its outlook, according to its earnings release.

Still, the comeback is fragile. ServiceNow sits less than 2% above its 2025 close of $153.19. It trades about 19% below its 52-week high of $192.97 and well above its low of $81.24.

title: Better Defense Stock to Own Through 2030: Palantir vs. RTX Corporation
detail:
Better Defense Stock to Own Through 2030: Palantir vs. RTX Corporation
Rick Orford, The Motley Fool
Tue, October 27, 2026 at 5:35 AM MST 4 min read
PLTR
RTX
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

With defense spending rising worldwide, Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR) and RTX Corporation (NYSE: RTX) offer two distinct ways to invest in the trend.

But which one deserves a spot in a portfolio through 2030: the fast-growing artificial intelligence (AI) software company or the established defense giant?

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
The software solution for modern warfare

Palantir's software helps defense and intelligence agencies gather information from diverse sources, coordinate operations, and inform battlefield decisions. With militaries becoming more reliant on drones, satellite imagery, and real-time intelligence, Palantir is building the software that makes it all possible.

AI is also making its role even more important. The company's Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP) helps organizations deploy AI using their own data and operational systems. And the results are showing up in the numbers.

In the second quarter, revenue climbed 93% year over year, with U.S. commercial revenue surging 149% and U.S. government revenue jumping 90%. The company also reported strong profitability and raised its full-year guidance. Looking ahead, if AI adoption accelerates, Palantir has more room to expand across both government and commercial markets.

But the catch is valuation: Palantir trades at a trailing price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 168. At that multiple, investors are paying a premium for software-driven growth.

On top of that, there are business risks. Palantir must compete with established technology providers, while government programs can be cut or canceled as budgets and priorities change.

Still, analyst opinion on the stock is bullish, with 30 analysts rating it a moderate buy. Their target prices during the next year, however, are between $80 and $265.

Meanwhile, another company offers a more traditional route into defense, with established products and a much broader business.

The defense giant with multiple ways to grow

Through Raytheon, Pratt & Whitney, and Collins Aerospace, RTX supplies everything from missile defense systems and military engines to aircraft components.

That breadth is a major advantage. Raytheon benefits from military demand for advanced air defense, precision weapons, and naval capabilities. Meanwhile, Pratt & Whitney and Collins Aerospace serve the global aviation industry.

Palantir Technologies Inc. (PLTR) is one of the stocks most watched by Zacks.com visitors lately. So, it might be a good idea to review some of the factors that might affect the near-term performance of the stock.

Shares of this company have returned +6.1% over the past month versus the Zacks S&P 500 composite's -0.8% change. The Zacks Internet - Software industry, to which Palantir Technologies belongs, has lost 6.6% over this period. Now the key question is: Where could the stock be headed in the near term?

While media releases or rumors about a substantial change in a company's business prospects usually make its stock 'trending' and lead to an immediate price change, there are always some fundamental facts that eventually dominate the buy-and-hold decision-making.

Earnings Estimate Revisions

Rather than focusing on anything else, we at Zacks prioritize evaluating the change in a company's earnings projection. This is because we believe the fair value for its stock is determined by the present value of its future stream of earnings.

Our analysis is essentially based on how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to take the latest business trends into account. When earnings estimates for a company go up, the fair value for its stock goes up as well. And when a stock's fair value is higher than its current market price, investors tend to buy the stock, resulting in its price moving upward. Because of this, empirical studies indicate a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and short-term stock price movements.

Palantir Technologies is expected to post earnings of $0.42 per share for the current quarter, representing a year-over-year change of +100%. Over the last 30 days, the Zacks Consensus Estimate has changed +0.2%.

The consensus earnings estimate of $1.64 for the current fiscal year indicates a year-over-year change of +118.7%. This estimate has changed +2.3% over the last 30 days.

For the next fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $2.33 indicates a change of +42.3% from what Palantir Technologies is expected to report a year ago. Over the past month, the estimate has changed +0.8%.

Having a strong externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool, the Zacks Rank, offers a more conclusive picture of a stock's price direction in the near term, since it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions. Due to the size of the recent change in the consensus estimate, along with three other factors related to earnings estimates, Palantir Technologies is rated Zacks Rank #3 (Hold).

DigitalOcean Holdings, Inc. (DOCN) is expected to deliver a year-over-year decline in earnings on higher revenues when it reports results for the quarter ended September 2026. This widely-known consensus outlook gives a good sense of the company's earnings picture, but how the actual results compare to these estimates is a powerful factor that could impact its near-term stock price.

The earnings report, which is expected to be released on November 3, might help the stock move higher if these key numbers are better than expectations. On the other hand, if they miss, the stock may move lower.

While management's discussion of business conditions on the earnings call will mostly determine the sustainability of the immediate price change and future earnings expectations, it's worth having a handicapping insight into the odds of a positive EPS surprise.

Zacks Consensus Estimate

This company is expected to post quarterly earnings of $0.32 per share in its upcoming report, which represents a year-over-year change of -40.7%.

Revenues are expected to be $307.24 million, up 33.8% from the year-ago quarter.

Estimate Revisions Trend

The consensus EPS estimate for the quarter has been revised 20% lower over the last 30 days to the current level. This is essentially a reflection of how the covering analysts have collectively reassessed their initial estimates over this period.

Investors should keep in mind that the direction of estimate revisions by each of the covering analysts may not always get reflected in the aggregate change.

Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise

Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise Chart for DOCN
Earnings Whisper

Estimate revisions ahead of a company's earnings release offer clues to the business conditions for the period whose results are coming out. Our proprietary surprise prediction model -- the Zacks Earnings ESP (Expected Surprise Prediction) -- has this insight at its core.

The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a more recent version of the Zacks Consensus EPS estimate. The idea here is that analysts revising their estimates right before an earnings release have the latest information, which could potentially be more accurate than what they and others contributing to the consensus had predicted earlier.

Thus, a positive or negative Earnings ESP reading theoretically indicates the likely deviation of the actual earnings from the consensus estimate. However, the model's predictive power is significant for positive ESP readings only.

The Aplos Data Vanguard: Elite promotion reshapes how Palantir rolls out Foundry and AIP, which is only part of today's story. Our analysis turns up 1 warning sign for Palantir Technologies as well.

Palantir Technologies builds data integration and analytics platforms that are widely used by intelligence and security agencies. A deeper U.S. partner network like Aplos Data effectively pushes those tools further into commercial sectors that work with sensitive or complex information.

2 things going right for Palantir Technologies that this headline doesn't cover.

Aplos partnership leans into Palantir Technologies' commercial AI catalyst, but raises execution bar

This Aplos Data move lines up squarely with the Palantir Technologies Narrative catalyst that depends on broader enterprise adoption of AIP and Foundry across commercial customers. Vanguard: Elite status effectively turns Aplos into a distribution and delivery arm inside the U.S., which supports the storyline about growing contract value and a wider commercial base alongside government work. At the same time, it puts more pressure on the risk side of that Narrative that flags reliance on a concentrated set of large contracts. A deeper partner tier only really helps if it converts into a thicker pipeline of varied clients rather than a few oversized wins.

Trading disclosure

Artificial intelligence (AI) has already created some spectacular winners on Wall Street. Palantir Technologies has surged roughly 1,100% over the last three years, while Snowflake has delivered a 119% return during the same period.

CrowdStrike (NASDAQ: CRWD) has had a good run as well, jumping more than 450% over the last three years and becoming one of Wall Street's biggest cybersecurity success stories. The growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) security could keep its business expanding for years.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

But there's a catch. Investors have already placed a whopping $264 billion valuation on the company, leaving little room for disappointment.

That creates an interesting question for investors looking for the next multibagger -- a stock that doubles, triples, or delivers even bigger returns.

Can CrowdStrike grow fast enough to justify its current valuation and still deliver those kinds of gains? The answer depends on two things: how quickly its business expands and how much investors are willing to pay for that growth.

Image source: Getty Images.
CrowdStrike's growth makes the case

CrowdStrike has established itself as a major player in cybersecurity through its Falcon platform, which helps businesses protect their computers, cloud applications, and sensitive information. As I recently highlighted, the growing adoption of AI is creating additional security challenges that could provide another source of long-term demand.

And CrowdStrike's existing business is already growing at an outstanding pace.

In its fiscal second quarter, which ended July 31, the company reported revenue of $1.47 billion, up 26% year over year. Annual recurring revenue (ARR) increased 25% to $5.84 billion, while net new ARR jumped 51% to a record $333 million.

Those numbers are encouraging. But they're especially interesting when you look at what CrowdStrike might become over the next five years. If the company maintains its current 25% annual ARR growth rate, its recurring revenue would reach approximately $17.8 billion in five years.

That's more than triple its current level.

Of course, maintaining 25% growth becomes increasingly difficult as a company gets bigger. CrowdStrike would need to add billions in new recurring revenue annually to sustain that pace. But the cybersecurity market continues to expand, and CrowdStrike has opportunities to sell additional security services to its existing customers.
